catalog_quote: 4.2.1 Although tone is phonemic in Huli, it carries a low functional load. In connected speech, it rarely appears to be crucial, but there are contrasting monosyllabic and disyllabic diads and triads in the language. [...] 4.2.2 Tone is problematic and warrants further investigation. The data collected so far show that there are four tones (tonemes) available for use, but that they are not employed in a uniform or consistent manner across the language group. Some speakers do not use pitch to discriminate between certain homophones, while others do. [...] 4.2.3 However, a point of near unanimity is that there are indeed four contrasting tones, which are: Tone 1 (falling): grave (a) / Tone 2 (rising): acute (a) / Tone 3 (level): macron (a) / Tone 4 (rising-falling): circumflex (a) [...] 4.3.4.1 Generally, at least one accented syllable in an inform[at]ion unit is given prominence, and this can be another source of tone perturbation. [...] 4.3.4.2 However, when more than one information unit occurs in an utterance, a speaker will typically accord salience to the one that he/she wishes to foreground. This is achieved by stepping up the pitch and increasing the loudness of the prominent syllable of that unit, other units being given a secondary prominence. Consider the following examples, in which a shadowed caret indicates a primary stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Huli is a tone language (Lomas: four contour tonemes, falling / rising / level / rising-falling, with low functional load and inconsistent use across speakers; SIL 1992 OPD and Pugh-Kitingan 2011: three word-tones, high-falling / mid-level / low-rising). Lomas gives no rule placing stress on a particular syllable of the word: prominence ('accent', 'primary stress' in his caret notation) is assigned at the level of the intonational information unit -- at least one accented syllable per unit, and the foregrounded unit's prominent syllable gets extra pitch and loudness (primary stress) while other units get secondary prominence. Stress appears in his segmental rules only as a conditioning feature ([+STRESS] in vowel allophony, 3.8.1.5, 3.11) and in the OPD only as 'certain non-stressed syllables' (p. 4); neither source states which syllable of a word is stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Lomas 1988 p. 83: when several information units occur in an utterance, the non-foregrounded units are 'given a secondary prominence' (phrase-level, not word-level).
new_statements.exceptions: Lomas 1988 p. 77: tones 'are not employed in a uniform or consistent manner across the language group. Some speakers do not use pitch to discriminate between certain homophones, while others do'; tones are perturbed in connected speech by intonation contours and by prominence (pp. 82-84). SIL OPD p. 3: 'The functional load of contrastive tone is not very high.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: tone (lexical, contrasting monosyllabic and disyllabic diads/triads such as i 'you sg.' vs i 'I', hale 'ear'/'tree sp.'/'torch', ma 'taro'/'neck'/'let's go'). Stress/accent statement is phrase-level only (information unit in connected speech, mingographic data); no citation-form or word-domain stress rule is given in any opened source.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Huli proper (huli1244). Lomas 1988 surveyed tone across 22 Huli locations (35 speakers) and bases the intonation/prominence description "mainly on data from the Gumu area" (a Huli dialect area, no separate glottocode); the SIL 1992 OPD is checked by "an expatriate speaker of Huli"; Pugh-Kitingan and the Rules worked at Tari. No differently named variety involved.

new_statements.quote: (p. 18, ch. 2 'Huli life and society', section 'Language') "To appreciate the analysis of musical examples in Part Two, further points should be noted. Huli is a full tone language employing three contrastive word tone patterns: high falling (/), mid level (—) and low rising (ˇ). Verb affixes have their own tonal patterns which are independent of those of verb stems (Rule and Rule 1970:x-xi, Rule 1977:10)." (p. 158, ch. 5 'Some Huli musical concepts', section 'Other Concepts') "They appear to have no concepts about rhythm or meter, however, and their music generally conveys no sense of metrical grouping. [...] Since stress is usually placed equally on each syllable in Huli speech, rhythm is determined largely by the rate of articulation."

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's classification of Huli as tonal (Lomas 1988) and adds an explicit word-stress statement the catalog lacks: stress is even across syllables (non-contrastive), i.e. no word-stress placement rule. Tone inventory differs in detail: Pugh-Kitingan (after Rule & Rule 1970, Rule 1977) gives THREE word-tone patterns (high-falling, mid-level, low-rising), whereas Lomas 1988 reports FOUR tones (falling, rising, level, rising-falling) with low functional load and speaker inconsistency; Lomas's 4.3.4 'prominence' is information-unit (phrase-level) accent, which is compatible with PK's 'stress placed equally on each syllable' at word level.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Huli is a tone language with three contrastive word-tone patterns (high-falling, mid-level, low-rising; verb affixes carry their own tone patterns), following Rule & Rule 1970 and Rule 1977; word stress is not contrastive: stress falls about equally on every syllable, so speech (and language-based music) has no metrical grouping and rhythm follows the rate of articulation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none described (stress said to be even across syllables).
new_statements.exceptions: 'usually' placed equally on each syllable (no exceptions spelled out); the orthography chart notes a reduced central-vowel allophone in 'non-stressed syllables' (after Rule & Rule 1970), implying some syllables are less stressed phonetically, without a placement rule. Sentence-terminating intonation (fall to a low pitch) is described throughout Part Two as overriding word-tone at line ends.
new_statements.identity_note: Huli as spoken across the Tari area, Southern Highlands (now Hela) Province; the author states (p. 17 n. 4) that Huli 'has no dialects. The language is spoken consistently throughout the entire area.' Fieldwork 1975-1978 (Bebenete, Wabia, Gugu, Hari Awi areas); phonology and tone analysis taken over from W. M. & J. E. Rule (APCM, Tari) 1970 and Rule 1977 (OLM 20).

sources.note: Ch. 3 segmental phonology (pp. 20-75) uses [+STRESS] as a conditioning feature in vowel-allophony rules (3.8.1.5, 3.11) but never states where stress falls; ch. 4 Prosodies: tone is phonemic, four contour tonemes, low functional load, inconsistent across speakers (4.2, p. 77); intonation 4.3: at least one accented syllable per information unit is given prominence; foregrounded unit gets primary stress by raised pitch and loudness, others secondary prominence (4.3.4.1-2, pp. 82-83); Appendix A tone survey (mingograms) mentions only mora prominence in diphthongs. No word-stress placement rule.
